utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: This is a hearing in IT-95-14-T in regard to orders I entered on February 14 1997 to ensure compliance with subpoenas duces tecum that I had also signed. May I have the appearances please for the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honor. My name is Mark Harmon. There is insufficient translation due to technical problems. Some discussion in the background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We will have to stand in recess for approximately five minutes for some technical problems to be adjusted,and if you will just be patient we will stand in recess for five minutes. (court in recess) (Court in session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Now once again let me verify that everyone can hear me. This is a hearing in IT-95-14-T in regard to orders that I entered to ensure compliance with the subpoena duces tecum on February 14th 1997. I apologise for the technical difficulties when are not using our courtroom we are always attempting to upgrade it and so we have been working on it and it appears that we are still working on it. But everyone can hear me now, and we are ready to proceed. May I have appearances please for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon your Honour. My name is Mark Harmon Appearing with me are my colleagues Mr Gregory Kehoe and Mr Andrew Cayley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: May I have appearances from this side, sir

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: I am Branko Salaj, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenatentory to the Court of Her Majesty, Queen of the Netherlands. If I may add I am here under a set of particular instructions which I hope that your Honour, will make it possible for me to read to the Record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you Ambassador Salaj. Appearances please

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Vasvija Vidovic. I attend this Session as the Representative of Bosnia Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And sir may I have your name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILJENIC
utterances.text: I am Orsat Miljenic for the Croatian Embassy, first Secretary

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Now Ambassador Salaj and Ms. Vidovic, and Mr Miljenic, you are not appearing today as Counsel and that’s why you are not dressed in robes. Very often Ms. Vidovic, you are here and you are in a robe, but today you are appearinghere as a representative but not as a legal counsel, so thank you for being here but that explains why the Prosecutor of course are dressed in their robes. Mr Harmon, would you like to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Pursuant to your Honour’s Court order of 14 February in which two additional orders were directed, one to the Republic of Croatia and one to Minister Susak, and a second to Bosnia Herzegovina and also to Mr Jelavic, I wish to report to the Court that there has been non-compliance with the subpoenas. We have not received a single document in relation to your order of 14 February 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Harmon, just by way of background then, on January 15 1997, in my capacity as the Confirming Judge for this indictment, I signed a subpoena duces tecum, two subpoenas duces tecum, one addressed to the Republic of Croatia and it was also addressed to the Defense Minister Susak. I signed a second subpoena duces tecum that was addressed to Bosnia Herzegovina and to Mr Ante Jelavic, the successor of the custodian of the records of the Central Archive of what was formerly the Ministry of Defense of the Croatian Community Herzec Bosna. I signed those subpoenas duces tecum as I indicated since I was the Confirming Judge, I had received the indictment, reviewed the evidence and then confirmed it. The subpoena directed the production of certain documents, some, Mr. Harmon you might help me, 12 were there, 13 I suppose......

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. In one subpoena there were 13 items requested and in the other subpoena there were approximately 19 items requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: A hearing then was held on February 14 1997 at 9:00 am and at that time the Prosecutor appeared and had indicated that there had been non compliance with the subpoena, the subpoena duces tecum directed directed to the Republic of Croatian and the Ministry of Defense, as to the subpoena duces tecum directed to Bosnia Herzegovinia and also directed to Mr Jelavic. As I recalled the Prosecutor stated that he has received some, I think it wa 11 items, a day or so before, that had been delivered not directly to the Prosecutor's Office but to an other party. And we then recessed and on that date, Ms. Vidovic, you appeared on behalf of Bosnia Herzegovina. There was no appearances on behalf of the Republic of Croatia. We then recessed, Ms. Vidovic, you then met with the Prosecutor in an attempt to review the documents that had been received to ascertain just what they were and whether they perhaps met a partial compliance. Then at the close of that day, I entered an order of non compliance. In that order of non compliance which I entered on February 14, the order was entitled “Order of a Judge to ensure compliance with subpoena duces tecum”. And let’s see I left out a piece regarding the Republic of Croatia, because the Republic of Croatia did respond by letter dated January 15 1997 to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, my attention setting out its position with respect to that subpoena duces tecum. We then entered an order to ensure compliance with the subpoena duces tecum addressed to the Republic of Croatia, also addressed to the Defence Minister Susak; and a second order that was addressed to Bosnia Herzegovina and to Mr Ante Jelavic. In that order, in those orders I directed that the Republic of Croatia is to ensure compliance with the subpoena duces tecum, which I entered on 15 June and directed to Defence Minister Susak to produce the documents described in the subpoena before February 19, 1997 at 2 pm, and I entered the same order with respect to Bosnia Herzegovina, except it was addressed to Mr Jelavic. If the items requested in the subpoena duces tecum then were not produced, then a representative of the Republic of Croatia and the Defence Minister, Susic, were to appear before me today at 2:00 pm to show cause for their non-compliance and to inform me how and when they will comply with this subpoena duces tecum, and once again the order was entered with respect to Bosnia Herzegovina directing a representative of Bosnia Herzegovina to appear and Mr Jelavic. So we are here today to hear from the parties regarding the order that I entered on February 14, 1997 to ensure compliance with the supoena duces tecum. I heard from Mr Vidovic when we last met and we had received the written reply from Croatia. Mr Harmon you have said there is no compliance at all. We haven’t received a document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not received a single document in support of your order directing production of these documents. I would like to inform the Court, in respect of the supoena that was directed to Mr Jelavic, that I have received from Madam Vidovic proof of service on the Cabinet of Mr Jelavic, and I would like to offer as part of the record these documents which Madam Vidovic has given to me and, I would, after I made my submission, ask her to explain what is in these documents. But, if I could have the usher please step forward and I’ll ask him to pass these documents to you. One is a document dated 15 February and served on the Cabinet of Mr Jelavic, if these could be made part of the Record, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is this proof of service of the order that was entered on 14 February?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That’s correct, your Honour. Madam Vidovic in just a moment, can explain what those documents are. I have to describe for your Honour another document, which I would also like to be admitted to the record. This is a document, that is a memo drafted by Mr Jos Paepen ,whose the Head of our Office in Zagreb. It is dated 19 February 1997 and it describes a meeting that Mr Paepen had this morning with a Mr Lucic, who is the Deputy of Mr Jelavic and I will ask the usher please pass a copy of this to you and this be made part of the record. The significance of this document, your honour, is that in essence, Mr Jelavic says: contrary to the proof of service that I have submitted in the previous submission, he says in this meeting with Mr Paeopen that he only received a notice of your order on 18 February 1997 when he was in Mostar. The third document that I would like to make part of the record is a document that was provided to me this afternoon by Madam Vidovic. This is a document, your Honour, that is signed by the Prime Minister of the Federation of Bosnia Herzegovina directing Mr Jelavic to comply with this Court order. And if I can ask the usher please tp provide this to you, your Honour. And then, your Honour, I would ask that perhaps the floor be given to Madam Vidovic to further expand on submission number 1 and submission number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, after the conclusion of the Court Session of 14 February 1997, I was handed a Court order to ensure compliance with the supoena deces tecum issued on 15 January 1997 by you, addressed to Mr Ante Jelavic, as the representative of the successor of the custodian of records belonging to the Archives of Herzeg Bosna and the military units of the Croatian Defence Council. The copies of the Court Order and the supoena to Mr Jelavic I forwarded them on the same date, 14 February 1997, to the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia Herzegovina with instructions to have them forwarded to Mr Jelavic, the Minister of Defence of the Federation and to Mr Mato Tadic, the Minister of Justice of the Federation of Bosnia Herzegovina, and to Mr Bicakcic, the Prime Minister of the Federation of Bosnia Herzegovina. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia Herzegovina in their letter of 14 February 1997 advised me that the Court Orders were submitted to the above-mentioned addresses and I received proof of service of the orders. Above all the proof of service to the Cabinet of Mr Ante Jelavic, indicating clearly that the Cabinet received the Court of order on 15 February 1997 at 12:45 pm. The Cabinet of Mr Mato Tadic and Mr Bicakcic, on the same day between 12 and 1pm.on the 15 February 1997. As additional proof of service, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs also submitted to me a copy of the protocol indicating that service was carried at the time I just mentioned. The same material that I already submitted to Mr Mark Harmon, I can submit to the Trial Chamber if necessary. Further more, I also received a letter from the Prime Minister of the Federation, Mr Edhem Bicakcic , indicating that he issued an order to the Ministry headed by Mr Jevolic asking him to meet fully the subpoena issued by the Trial Chamber, and to take every measure necessary to have the said documents handed over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Ms Vidovic, are you, in your capacity as the, I am trying to think of your exact title, liaison with the International Tribunal for Bosnia Herzegovina, are you contesting the authority of the Tribunal to issue this subpoena duces tecum or the order that was entered on February 14?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do not contest this right of the Tribunal to issue such subpoena because Bosnia Herzegovina has signed an agreement with the International Tribunal on cooperation, and pursuant to that agreement, the International Tribunal has the right to issue such orders and subpoenas and I also think that it is in keeping with the Statute of the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you Ms Vidovic. Mr Harmon, it appears then what needs to be resolved, and if you wish Ms Vidovic, you may make those documents part of the record and of course, Mr Harmon the request that you made to have these documents part of the record, is granted. What remains then with respect to Bosnia Herzegovina I gather, is sitting together and see if the document will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a suggestion? An that is,given the proof of service that I have submitted to Your Honour showing that the Cabinet of Mr Jelavic received your order, earlier than is claimed in the memorandum of Mr Paepen. Mr Paepen says Mr Jelavic’s representative informed him received the order only yesterday. To give Mr Jelavic the benefit of the doubt, I would request Your Honour, that this Court issue a similar order that it issued on 14 February in the same terms, and that it direct Mr Jelavic or his representative, his qualified representative, in the same terms as your previous order, to appear before you on Monday 24 February at 9am to explain what efforts have been made to comply with the court order and to furnish to this Court a schedule of compliance. The second request I make, Your Honour, is in respect of the letter of Mr Paepen. While I firmly believe that the proper service of documents of this Court is on the representative of Bosnia Herzegovina, Mr Paepen’s memo that I submitted to this Court, describes a fax number for Mr Jelavic and my request, so there is no disagreement or misunderstanding or any question at all, that the Registrar be directed to fax to that number a copy of any new order that you issue, In addition to serving that same order on the Bosnian Herzegovinian Embassy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: This order should it not be directed to Bosnia Herzegovina and also directed to Mr Jelavic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: OK. And on the 24 February, perhaps we will begin at 10am instead of 9am..

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Today is 19, and that is how many business days from now. Let’s see. You see Mr Harmon there is no need to make an early setting if it is just for the purpose of someone appearing saying ‘we don’t have them yet, but we are making a good effort to locate the documents. So, I want to give sufficient time. Now I understand the first subpoena, the subpoena deces tecum, was issued January, what was it January 17, (Mr. Harmon: 15th, your Honour) 15. So, as you said at the last hearing, if they have started gathering the materials, they would be in a position to know whether they either have them or will not have them - or may make some sort of an objection regarding producing them and you think that can be done by 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would think so, your Honour, given the fact that they have had well over a month to engage in this exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Ms Vidovic, how does that setting meet with your schedule - setting that for February 19. I mean February 24, Monday?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is allrigth with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That order will be entered. I’ll talk a little bit more though about my role in any future proceedings regarding the subpoenas duces tecum, but the order will be entered by me. OK. Does that conclude then the Prosecutor’s submission regarding Bosnia Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes,it does, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, regarding the Republic of Croatia, as best as I can recall I set up the background. Mr Salaj, I do have a written response, or a written response, from Croatia that was signed by Mr Jelenic..(MR> SALAJ: Jelenic) Would then you like to proceed to respond to the Prosecutor’s position regarding the Republic of Croatia and this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: As I said initially, Your Honour, I would very much like to record with your permission a prepared statement on the position of Croatia, but I would like to do it in Croatian if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You will then read the statement and, if necessary, it can be made part of the record as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Your Honour, my appearance here today in the capacity of the representative of the Republic of Croatia is an expression of respect to you personally and to the Tribunal as a whole, and also an expression of the willingness on the part of the Republic of Croatia to cooperate. The government of the Republic of Croatia is surprised by the form of the subpoena of January 15, 1997. In our view, it is not founded in the international law, nor on the statute and the rules of this Tribunal. These instruments do not form a basis for decision whereby states and their representatives could be issued subpoenas which are Court orders where compliance must be done under pain of punishment. Had the Security Council intented to depart so far from the international law, the provisions on subpoenas would be expressly stipulated and not left to the interpretation of the Tribunal itself. Furthermore, the Republic of Croatia as any other sovereign state determines itself who will represent it. When it comes to the cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal, it is the Croatian governement. In other words, its office for cooperation with the Tribunal, so that requests can be addressed only to these institutions, not to individual officials in person. Since the Republic of Croatia cannot accept a subpoena as the manner of communicating of the Tribunal with sovereign states, it cannot consider Court orders formulated in this manner. However, the Croation governement is aware of its obligations to cooperate with the International Criminal Tribunal and it is prepared to meet the requests pursuant to its constitutional act on cooperation with the Tribunal, the statute and the rules of the Tribunal, the international law as well as the principles recognized by the international community. Since it is aware of its obligations and despite the fact that the Prosecutor has not tried to obtain the said documents in some other acceptable manner, but has decided to issue a subpoena right away, the Republic of Croatia has taken every step to avoid such a situation which is damaging to the Republic of Croatia but also to the office of the Prosecutor and to the Tribunal itself. The situation is particularly unacceptable to General Blaskic, a man who has voluntarily placed himself at the disposal of the Tribunal and who has been waiting for almost a year in detention for his trial to begin. The Republic of Croatia has gone so far as to offer a comprise to the Prosecutor. If the Prosecutor gives up the subpoena, Croatia will as soon as possible initiate the process of meeting the requests. In this sense, we propose that Croatian experts meet as soon as possible the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor to consider possibilities in which this request can be met. The Office of the Prosecutor has rejected this proposal. All this has led us to the conclusion that, in order to improve the cooperation and the overall operation of the Tribunal, the issue whether subpoenas can be issued to sovereign states should be brought up before the Security Council of the United Nations for its consideration. Thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Harmon, do you have anything in response?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thankyou, your Honour, and thank you Ambassador Salaj for expounding your position. Your Honour, this subpoena that was issued by your Honour, was issued on January 15 1997 and as I mentioned to you at the last hearing, I received no communication whatsoever from the Government of Croatia, prior to receiving the written reply to the subpoena duces tecum that is dated the 15th of, that is date the day of hearing that we had on the last occasion. What is significant about that document, your Honour, is there is a statement contained in paragraph 9 of that document, indicating that Croatia does in fact possessed documents that are relevant and responsive to the Tribunal’s request and to the Prosecutor’s request and they have made a determination, based on that paragraph, that those aren’t relevant to General Blaskic. The position of the Prosecutor clearly is, your Honour, that we are the party who will decide the relevance of those particular documents not the Republic of Croatia. Now, this Court can issue a subpoena, that it is legally binding and that the Republic of Croatia is obligated to honour that Court order. If the Republic of Croatia and, I want to clarify their position, if they are saying they have absolutely no intention whatsoever of complying with this subpoena, period, then I will take one view. If they are saying that this Court does not have the power or jurisdiction to issue a subpoena, and they are prepared to brief that and present legal submissions to your Honour, then I would take a different position. I would respectfully request, your Honour, that there be clarification on that particular point. My view is, your Honour, that if they are saying the latter, we are prepared to submit and suggest to your Honour a briefing schedule to litigate the issue of the legality of the subpoena. My proposal, I can submit some dates to your Honour, I would also add that parenthetically, your Honour, that while the Republic of Croatia has repeatedly express their willingness to comply with providing the Office of the Prosecutor with those documents, there is nothing, pending any litigation that would prevent them from making compliance with the items that are listed in the subpoena and which they admit, in their reply to the subpoena duces tecum, that they possess. The fact that there is a legal dispute, should not prevent them, in their good will to provide us with the documents that they say they possess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Harmon, does that conclude your submission regarding that point. Ambassador Salaj, do you wish to respond to that or stand by your statement or what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: (JUDGE MCDONALD: Turn on your microphone, sir) Your Honour, I do not think that I really can go beyond my brief and I think that it has been clear enough even on the point raised by Mr Harmon. We believe that should the Security Council of the United Nations have envisaged the possibility of subpoenas to the states, it would have said so in its decision. That is the position of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me intercede if I may. The response that was received from the Republic of Croatia on January 15 in paragraph 9, I don’t know that it goes as far as you may have been summarizing, Mr Harmon, but it says that: “In its request, the Tribunal orders the provision of numerous documentation and information. The number of information and documents is huge and surprising, due to the fact that some of the requested documents do not even exist. Others do exist but cannot be related to the case of General Blaskic. And yet others perhaps do exist, but are not in the possession of the authorities of the Republic of Croatia, because they relate to activities in Bosnia Herzegovina. So I don’t know that if the position has been stated that none of the documents are relevant. They really have three points: either that the documents do not exist, that they cannot be related to the case of General Blaskic, and then yet perhaps others do exist but are not in their possession. So, I don’t know that they are as firm as you might suggest regarding those documents. Even if they are in the possession of Bosnia, not in the possession of the Republic of Croatia because they relate to activities in Bosnia Herzegovina, there is a possibility that perhaps, with good will and with a sincere effort that those documents could be located, even though they may not be in the Republic of Croatia due to whatever relationship may exist between the Republic of Croatia and other areas. So I don’t know that they are taking that firm position, but of course though Ambassador Salaj does say that the statute does not allow for the Tribunal, one to issue subpoenas, and secondly does not allow for the Tribunal to issue subpoenas directed to individuals within a state but instead should be directed to the state itself. And those are very serious legal points that, my review of the statute and of our rules would lead me to a different conclusion, but I haven’t had the benefit of briefing, because article 18.2 of the statute says that the Tribunal, that the Prosecutor shall have the power to question suspects, etc. and seek the assistance of the state authorities concerned. And then in 19.2, of the statute, it says “upon confirmation of an indictment, the judge may, at the request of the Prosecutor, issued such orders and warrant for the arrest detention surrender or transfert of persons, and any other order as maybe required for the conduct of the trial and subpoena duces tecums are normally issued for the conduct of the trial and then of course in our rules itself, Rule 54 of our rules of the Tribunal’s rules provide that “a judge or a trial chamber may issue orders, summons, subpoenas, warrants and transfert orders as maybe necessary for the purpose of the investigations of preparation of the conduct of the trial”. So it’s there in our rules, you would argue that somehow our rules go beyond the statute and that would be a legal point, and you would suggest that we ask the Security Council to resolve this. The Security Council is very busy in our creation. We were created as an independent body and I don’t know that the Security Council is the appropriate body to interpret our laws, our rules of procedure. Perhaps you could look through the submissions that were made by the various states when the Tribunal was created and get some guidance. I don’t know whether we want to ask the Security Council for that. It seems to me that we need to solve a problem, Mr Harmon, and perhaps we have a solution on the table so to speak. Do we not have a solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One solution, your Honour, is to brief the legal point on the schedule that I am prepared to suggest. (JUDGE MCDONALD: OK) And certainly the Court, your Honour, will prepare to litigate that issue. We certainly aren’t prepared to wait for the Security Council to resolve this issue. The compromise, your Honour, that has been suggested is a compromise that was suggested - I understand I wasn’t party to this conversation at all - may have been suggested yesterday. But we have been at this effort, your Honour, to secure relevant documents for over a month. We have a trial date that will be coming up very shortly. That is important Your Honour, that the Republic of Croatia fulfill its obligation to cooperate with the Tribunal under article 29. And it should fulfill that obligation, your Honour, by producing the documents that are relevant, that have been identified in the subpoena and that we havebeen anxiously awaiting since January 15. I think the answer, with all due respect to Mr Salaj and to the Republic of Croatia, that we will not respond, we will not litigate, we will not produce the document, is not an adequate response from our point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Tribunal provides in article 3 that requests for cooperation or enforcement of a decision of the Tribunal shall be forwarded to the Government of the Republic of Croatia. You understand that the subpoena duces tecum was forwarded to the Republic of Croatia. It was also forwarded to the Minister of Defence. Yes, Ambassador Salaj

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Your Honour, it should be very much stressed that I am talking about subpoenas directed to Governments. We do not question a supoenas to individual citizens or persons whom the Tribunal is interested in, but not to governments and its officials. That is a basic difference, I think, for us and we stand there. I cannot understand, I can’t go into pleading any further our cause, but I am very surprised by what the Prosecution says here about our not cooperating. We have offered our full cooperation but some others statute and the one that has been evoked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Then in the agreement it provides that the request for cooperation or enforcement of a decision of the Tribunal shall be granted by the Government of the Republic of Croatia, if the request or decision is founded on appropriate provisions of the statute and rules of procedure in evidence of the Tribunal. If I understand what you are saying is, that even if the subpoena duces tecum was never even addressed to the Minister of Defence, it had just been addressed to the Republic of Croatia, if the Republic considers that subpoenas duces tecum are not appropriate, and are not allowed under the statute and rules, then it seems to me that the issue that you raised about it, should not be addressed to individuals, is really a non issue because if you would not have passed it on to the Authority if you felt that the Tribunal was without authority. Do you understand what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Not quite. It is a long reasoning, but I missed it somewhere in the middle, I am terribly sorry. Some how, I hope that I made the opposition clear. Should, in order for Court to be able to issue subpoenas to Government, this possibility should have been mentioned in the decision of the Security Council. That is our position very simply. And really as a response to your question, if I recall it, if it was not directed to Mr Susak..., but to the Republic of Croatia, we could not serve it because we do not respond to subpoenas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: But I understand that you are willing to make an accomodation in this instance, notwithstanding the request being made by subponea to provide the document. How long do you anticipate you would need to complete the review of the request of the documents, if you have began and provide those that you consider relevant to the Prosecution? How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really can’t give you a precise answer for the simple reason that this document that we have received really is not a very simple document, it is an extremely wide ranging set of requests. What we would have tried to suggest to the Office of the Prosecutor, is that their people and ours sit down and see in a very simple manner. We have not received any other request in this matter, other than just being served a subponea. And permit me to say, this is somewhat unusual way of opening or trying to get what you need of a government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: When would you be prepared to sit down with the Prosecutor and a representative who has sufficient knowledge of the documents to be familiar with them? When would that person be willing to sit down with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: We have said, the sooner the better, and we would even suggest that perhaps these discussions be held in Zagreb because they are so many different materials that perhaps they should, you know, they would be discussing with several people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Monday, how about Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: See I can’t.... You know the position that I am in. I either have to act and rule according to the law or I can attempt to reach a compromise with the parties, trying to get to where you want to get to without our making a legal decision. I am prepared to make a legal decision because I have reviewed the authorities myself. But I am trying as best as I can to reach a compromise. Monday ? If they are in Zagreb, would you sit down or have the person who is familiar with these documents sit down with the Prosecution? That is an easy solution I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Madame, I am not trying to escape committing myself. It is only the problem of, it is really posing a pratical problem because that is something we have been proposing yesterday and I was not given a positive reply by the Office of the Prosecutor and I never pursued it any further with Zagreb for simple reasons that it was not available to us. I would have to contact Zagreb and.....

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: How long would it take you today to contact Zagreb to get a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: I don’t know. It is. How long time do governements take to get a proper response from their bureaucracy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Well, I don’t know. I don’t know your bureaucracy and some are different than others depending on what their goals are. But it seems to me that the Minister of Defence, from what I heard about the documents that have been asked for and his role, if he is available near a telephone, he could give a response. Now if there are other requirements that you would have to go through, to even determine whether you could sit down, then I am misunderstanding you. Because as I understand, you are offering to sit down with the Prosecutor and go over this request.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: OK Now what I need from you is a date when you are willing to do that. And if I don’t get a date, then I don’t know what to do except take this legal issue right on, which is fine with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Well, I don’t know, my suggestion, I think that it should be workable that a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor visits Zagreb next week for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me suggest this and sort of thinking out loud. If the Prosecutor can report back and if Mr Salaj, not necessarily you, maybe Mr Meijic, a representative, on Monday to report back, either report back in person or advise by letter that we would receive on the 24th, Monday 24, setting a specific date for the appropriate representatives of the Republic of Croatia to sit with the Prosecutor and go over the request for documents. So that you would report back by Monday, 24 February, providing a specific date, not as soon as possible or anything like that - but a specific date. Is this acceptable? Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I hope so. These things are not entirely under my control, but I will do my best to ensure that it will happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I know very well that orders can be sent to the government of Croatia and if subpoenas fit within there, I don’t want to put myself in a position of ordering the Republic of Croatia to report back on 24th. I will accept a response from you if you will tell me that you will do that. You can report back on 24th with a specific date, can’t you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Well Madame, I hope that we understand each other. This is not under the statute of subpoena, but rather of some kind of separate order that you would issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I don’t want to enter an order. What I want you to do is to tell me that the compromise that you are proposing is to have the appropriate representatives that is persons who knowledge of the document to sit with the Prosecutor, go over the request, and make a determination as to which one they will give, either yes, or no, yes, no. In this way, we put beyond part of the problem and that is all what I want from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: This discussion cannot I am afraid, take place under the statute of subponea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What are you saying? I am not asking for it to take place under the statute. This is a compromise. I can suspend this order that I have entered, pending a report back from you on Monday 24 February advising of the date on which this meeting will take place and I will suspend the order. And then when I suspend the order, what happens is that the good will of Croatia is motivating this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: You see, it puts me in an unclear position as to what to report to Zagreb, as to where we stand in this particular issue. We would like to cooperate, I have maintained it now several times, and will be as practical as possible but there cannot be a shadow or doubt that this is made under any kind of threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Except that I am not a diplomat Mr Salaj. I am just a judge and I just go by the rules so I am not really in a position to talk about that. What I am attempting to do is to reach a resolution of this issue. I truly am, because if we don’t move forward with real cooperation, this Tribunal will be crippled. We have 74 indictees, 7 in custody, 2 have been turned over by Bosnia Herzegovina and if we do not get cooperation from countries, not a willingness to cooperate or a desire to cooperate, but actual cooperation, then we all fail. And we all fail together, that is you, me, everyone. So rather than deal with technicalities, I am telling you that if I enter an order suspending this order and stating that it is suspended, that the Republic of Croatia has challenged the legality of it; however the Republic of Croatia is willing as it has always been willing - if that is the language you want me to put in - to cooperate and as evidence of this cooperation, they will meet with the Prosecution on a particular date to discuss the request. Now the Prosecutor does not want that compromise, and I am suggesting it only as a way to reach the bottom line, but it is really out of my province. Because my province is really just to rule on matters of law and I am ready to rule, really. I don’t need briefing. So this is what I am suggesting that you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I need time to consider the proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We stand in recess. How long do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Half an hour. and you understand then the parameters I am talking about. Do you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Yes, the problem would not rise at all if somehow the subponea question was quashed and we had a complete situation of..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I cannot quash the subponea, because then I do is that I give up the authority that I have already assumed by assigning the subponea and the order. I cannot quash it, but I can certainly suspend its operation, recognizing the response of Croatia that it is illegal, for the reasons that you have stated and, therefore suspending its operation incoperating... you know as we discussed the cooperation. I think that’s pretty reasonable. I am not a diplomat, it sounds like a pretty good arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Well being a.. It is always an advantage to be a lady and a judge. Diplomats are very weird and formalistic people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for thirty minutes and keep in mind that what we want to do is to get to the bottom of this problem. And I understand your position very well and I don’t want to put you in a difficult position but understand the position that I have as well. What we want to do is to get to the bottom of obtaining this document. And we will stand in recess for thirty minutes. (Court stands in recess for 30 minutes)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Ambassador Salaj. Have you been able to make the necessary arrangements?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, not all the arrangements that I would have liked to make, it is a very short time. I think, however, that we could proceed in a manner which you have suggested, but we have a few simple reservations which I hope you will find agreeable. One of them is that I repeat that the Republic of Croatia does not accept subponeas to governments, but you have given us assurances that you have taken note of the position of Croatia about that. We would like it to be understood that a meeting of Croatian experts and representatives of the Prosecutor’s Office, will take place only as an expresssion of the Croatian wish to cooperate with the ICTY. And we would appreciate that the Office of the Prosecutor provides the Croatian authorities with the list of requested documents but not a titulated subponeas but a text that really would retake what they would like to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, in a form of letter for example. MR SALAJ....: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: OK. MR> SALAJ: And I have really not been able to ascertain the exact time of when this meeting could take place but I would inform you as you suggested, on Monday about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What I suggested on Monday was to inform me of the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Inform me on February 24 of the exact date for this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Does that conclude your remarks Mr Salaj. Thank you. Mr Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be brief but to the point. Since January 15, clearly we have been requesting these documents that we believe to be relevant and necessary and would be helpful to the Trial Chamber in deciding the issues that we will be facing in the trial of General Blaskic. We are genuinely interested in the production of those documents. I have absolutely no problem with providing the Republic of Croatia with an other version of the substance of what is contained in that subponea, because I view the subponea as a request for assistance from the Croatian government directed through this Court. However, I will be glad to prepare a letter today, which I can serve on Ambassador Salaj today, with a request for assistance in the form that we have requested since January 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The request for assistance - I think what Ambassador Salaj is suggesting would just be a letter, and it will be decided to whom it will be directed... MR SALAJ.....: - inaudible -

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now Your Honour, what I wish to avoid, since I have a trial date, that will be coming up very shortly, is to engage in protracted negociations on modalities of how and under what circumstances, documents could be seen and reviewed. What I need very frankly, and what I requested for over a month, are the documents themselves and I think it is absolutely imperative that there be meaningful production if we are to engage in this step. Otherwise there is valuable time lost and we are engaged in empty rhetoric. My own view, Your Honour, is that I would request that there be a hearing on 28 February at 2:00 pm before Your Honour, in which the Prosecutor can report whether there has been meaningful production of documents that will be contained in our request for assistance. In the event there has not,your Honour, we will be making an appropriate request in respect of lifting of the subponea, lifting the suspension of the subponea. Your Honour, there is one additional request and that is: if we wait until 24 Feb, then we protacted the process unnecessarily and it seems to me that perhaps, Ambassador Salaj could report back earlier than next Monday on where and when the Prosecutor’s office could meet with the representative of the Croatian governement. My suggestion, Your Honour, would be that the Croatian Ambassador could report to this Court on Friday, this Friday, on where and when the meeting could take place. That would permit Mr Salaj more than ample time to contact his government and confirm that his government is prepared to engage in a meaningful compromise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Ambassador Salaj has made that effort and 24 February as his earliest day. Is that correct Ambassador Salaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Yes Your Honour. Something that amazes me really is that the Prosecutor is in such a hurry after 16 months that he has indicted a person. We are talking about material which should, theoretically, be truck loads and truck loads of paper, because in all bureaucracies and even Croatia, there are papers and it is a highly technical job to discerne what, in all that the Prosecution has required, is sensible thing to ask. I will be very plain on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Two questions really. Mr Harmon, how would you envision this hearing on 28 Feb. to proceed, you said for the Prosecutor to report as to meaningful production, would that be an ex-parte, would you just report and advise a judge as what has been produced?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also request a representative of the Republic of Croatia be present as well, if there is a dispute as to our report, I would invite the Republic of Croatia to take issue with our presentation at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Ambassodor Salaj

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Not being a legal expert, I can only offer you my personal view that the material as such is going to take some time and I think the joint effort by the Prosecution, if the Prosecution wants to really to get whatever documents are necessary and we can give them in time. It seems to me that we are rushing and in a way which as I say from the beginning was not acceptable to the Republic of Croatia. The rushing without having tested her willingness to assist really in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Testing whose willingness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: I sorry

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Oh, Testing whose willingness. You’re saying because the subpoena was issued without the willingness

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Croatia’s willingness to assist

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I don’t know what was done before the subpoena, let me just comment on this. The meeting that would take place, you are then to advise the Court on Feb 24 of the exact date of the meeting, now what I don’t want to happen is that the notice will say, well the meeting will take place soon, or the meeting will take place in April.or May, or June. It has to be done with some dispatch. What I suggest is that you at least have a meeting, so that even if, when you return to Croatia, I mean when you contact the appropriate representatives in Croatia, it is determined that there are truck loads of material and we don’t know when we can meet to provide them in the appropriate order, or we need to go through this material to see what needs to be provided. That to be avoided, and that instead there be a meeting between the appropriate representatives and the Prosecutor, regardless of whether you have truck loads or regardless whether you have one or two documents - there be a meeting on a specific date to discuss that. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Oh yes. That is exactly my meaning, but, you see, the problem that I have with the date of 28 is really that this would mean, that they would not only meet but they would also have resolved whatever sort of thorny questions there may be and I am really thinking of a joint effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: OK. Your comment really goes to whether or not we should not have a hearing on 28 Feb. And what I am concerned about is that when you report back on 24, that you give a specific date, so that the meeting can be held. Now it seems to me that the meeting could be held within a week’s time if you report back on 24, certainly a meeting be arranged between the two sometime during that week?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: I certainly hope so. But what I have seen I expect them not just to meet and say hello to each other but rather to have very substantive meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: OK. And what I am suggesting is that they have a meeting early that week, even if it is necessary to say hello and then to begin to explore at the very least, the scope of this material that you say it exists and I don’t want the first meeting to be delayed because of the volume of the material, so I would suggest that a meeting be held during that week of 24, so that you can set some preliminary rules, perhaps discuss informally the material that is available, that kind of thing. There shouldn’t be a problem with that, as far as I see it. It should be more than a meeting to say hello, but still one to talk about how we are going to produce these records, even if an other meeting then has to be held to go thru the records, whatever is necessary. So I hope that you can set that meeting by February 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I think we completely agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: OK. So you set that day for the first meeting before the end of February 28. Now as far as the Prosecutor then reporting back, either alone or with a representative of Croatia, at that point we will be moving into an area where a judge will have to consider, hopefully, whether the documents that have been produced, and I am hoping that some will be produced, I have all faith that some will be produced during that first meeting. Then though, a Judge is going to have to consider whether or not these documents or some of these documents are as you said, Mr Harmon, helpful to the Trial Chamber in resolving the issues of Blaskic. Now under Rule 54, of course of our rules, I signed the subpoena and I am perfectly authorized to conduct this hearing to this point, but I would suggest that thereafter these matters regarding the content of the material that is provided and the relevance, etc.... be handled by the Trial Chamber that is trying the case and that would be either Judge Jorda, whose is the Presiding Judge, or the entire Trial Chamber. I am not in a position to make a determination as to whether, if it is contested, that there are certain documents that are relevant to or helpful to resolving the issue of the Blaskic trial, because that is not my trial. And I think at that point, the other Trial Chamber should take over or or one of the other Judges from the Trial Chamber, probably the President Judge. So, I will then carry this through to this point, but then once the exchange begins - and I am very hopeful that there will be an exchange - that Judge Jorda handle the matter of whether or not there has been substantial compliance, whether the documents are relevant, some maybe, some may not to the issue of Blaskic trial, because that is not my trial. So, as far as a hearing on 28 Feb. I will at this time deny that request. I expect that the parties will meet the week of 24, you will advise Ambassador Salaj me of the exact date of the meeting but I expect it will be 28 the preliminary meeting if that ‘s all it is, and then when you begin the exchange process, it seems to me that it will then be handled by the other Trial Chamber because I am not the appropriate judge to resolve that issue. I will suspend the order of Feb 14 that I entered to enssure compliance with the subpoena duces tecum. I will in that order note that the Republic of Croatia has challenged the legality of it, and that in a cooperative spirit, in its willingness to cooperate, they are willing to work informally with the Prosecutor to provide documents that have been requested. We also though need to resolve the matter regarding Bosnia Herzegovina and you had indicated in respect to that, Mr Harmon, that an order be entered setting a hearing for February 24 at 2:00 pm. Is that correct? MR HARMON At 10.00 o’clock your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I had requested that you enter an order similar to the order you entered 14 February in respect of Mr Jelavic and Bosnia Herzegovina and that you direct Mr Jelavic or his representative to appear before you on 24 February at 10:00 am. It also requested, your Honour, that the Registrar, supoena, not subpoena, I am sorry, fax to Mr Jelavic at the telephone number that is contained in the memorandum of Mr Paepen a copy of your order as well as serve a copy of the new order on Bosnia Herzegovina Embassy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: An order will be entered. The exact content of the order, of course, will await my drafting of it but we will set that date, Ms. Vidovic for Feb 24 at 10:00am and the order should be issued today or tomorrow. I do believe that is all what we need to resolve today. Is that correct Mr Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there anything else, Ambassador Salaj? Ms Vidovic? Is there anything further? (Both Answer in the negative)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you everyone for coming and working in this cooperative spirit and I except it will be very successful..
